nameStory: The windowpane flounder gets its distinctive name from its remarkably thin, almost translucent body that you can practically see through like a pane of glass. When held up to the light, this flatfish is so thin and semi-transparent that it resembles a window made of frosted glass, especially around the edges.
description: The windowpane flounder is a unique flatfish that looks like nature decided to create a living pancake. Both eyes are positioned on one side of its flattened body, allowing it to lie flat on the ocean bottom while keeping watch for prey and predators above. These fish can grow up to about 18 inches long and are remarkably thin and lightweight for their size, feeling almost papery when handled.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened and nearly translucent body that feels thin and delicate, like wet parchment paper, with both eyes on the same side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale brown to grayish coloration on the eye side with darker mottled patterns, while the blind side is white or cream-colored

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal and anal fins that run almost the entire length of the body, creating a continuous fringe around the fish

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 8-12 inches long but can reach up to 18 inches, surprisingly lightweight for their size due to their thin profile

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found on sandy or muddy bottoms in relatively shallow coastal waters, often partially buried with just their eyes exposed

habitat: Windowpane flounders inhabit the sandy and muddy bottoms of New England's coastal waters, typically at depths between 15-240 feet. They prefer areas with soft substrates where they can easily bury themselves, commonly found in bays, harbors, and along the continental shelf from shallow nearshore waters to moderate depths.

seasonality.spring: Fish begin moving into shallower waters as temperatures warm, making them more accessible to shore-based anglers. Spawning activity increases during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for encountering windowpane flounders in shallow coastal waters and bays. They're most active and easiest to observe during warmer months.
seasonality.fall: Fish remain active but begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool. Still commonly caught during this season.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper, warmer waters offshore, becoming less common in shallow areas typically accessed by recreational fishers.

funFact: Windowpane flounders are born looking like normal fish with eyes on both sides of their head, but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across their skull to join the other eye on one side - a transformation so dramatic it seems like science fiction!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small flatfish like winter flounder, but windowpane flounders are much thinner and more translucent. Remember: if you can almost see through it like a window, it's probably a windowpane flounder.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'flounder,' windowpane flounders actually belong to the turbot family rather than the true flounder family, which can cause confusion among anglers and even some field guides that group all flatfish together.
compareHints: Since windowpane flounder is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to other local flatfish like winter flounder and summer flounder. Windowpane flounders are distinctively thinner and more translucent than these relatives, and lack the pronounced thickness and solid feel of true flounders.
